title: Ang 1125: Bhairao begins
hookLine: Guru Nanak opens the serious morning raga
tomorrow: why would a hymn about pride need a potter?

lines: TEN TO SEVEN, DAY ONE OF CAMP.
A KID CRYING IN THE BACK.
cards: Ten to seven, a gurdwara hall, folding tables still stacked against the wall. A row of sleepy kids in socks: day one of summer camp.

The camp leader hands a sixteen-year-old counselor a book of hymns, open to a raga she barely knows, and says: you start us off. Her hands are cold. In the back, a little boy is crying because his mom just drove away.
The heading on the page says Bhairao. She looks at the first line, and it seems like a strange thing to sing to a crying kid at seven in the morning. So what does it say?

teach.b: The first line, on ang 1125, is Guru Nanak's. In paraphrase: nothing happens outside of you. You make it, you watch over it, you know it.
A little further: what can I say? Nothing can be said. Whatever is, is your will.
That's how Bhairao begins, a serious raga that tradition sings in the early morning. Notice what it doesn't do. It doesn't start with a request.
No help me get through today.

teach.h: NOT A REQUEST. A BIGGER ROOM.
teach.b: It starts by making the room bigger. The crying kid, the cold hands, the mom driving off to work: none of it sits outside the One the hymn is speaking to.

teach.h: HUKAM, AND A SHRUG OF WONDER.
teach.b: Sikhs call that order hukam, and Guru Nanak's answer to it here isn't a lecture. It's wonder: what can I say? Here's something to tell a friend tonight.
The Granth isn't sorted by Guru first.

teach.h: SORTED BY RAGA, THEN BY GURU.
teach.b: It's sorted by raga, by musical mood, and inside each raga the Gurus mostly come in order, Guru Nanak first.
So when you turn from Kedara to Bhairao, the evening is over, and the first voice of the morning is his again. Back in the hall, the counselor sings the line. It doesn't fix the crying.
She waves the boy up to sit beside her on the floor, where he can watch her hands. Nothing outside of you, including him.

how: Ragis sing the Bhairao hymns in kirtan, often in the early morning; readers find Guru Nanak's hymns by the heading Mahala 1 at the start of the raga.

games.q: the first page of Bhairao — tap the pairs.
p: a serious raga sung in the morning
the first voice in the raga

s: the Granth groups its hymns by raga before it groups them by Guru
inside each raga the Gurus mostly come in order, so Bhairao opens with Guru Nanak.
Bhairao's first hymn opens with a request for help
it opens with wonder: nothing happens outside of you; what can I say?
if everything is inside God's order, nothing you do matters
the hymn widens the room; it never says every action is fine.

games.q: first day at a new job. your manager hands you a task you've never done, in front of everyone. Bhairao's first line is in your head. which reading of it helps?
o: nothing here is outside the One, me included; begin, and learn as you go.
it's all God's will, so if it goes wrong, none of it is on me.
stay quiet until I've worked out the perfect way to do it.
games.why: the hymn widens the room without excusing anyone: hukam is the order everything moves in, and the counselor still had to sing the first line.

practice: For this sit, listen for one sound in the room you hadn't noticed: a fan, a bird, a car, your own breath. Don't call it good or bad. Let it be inside the room with you, the way the hymn lets everything be inside the One.
If you'd like, read ang 1125 before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1125. Where Bhairao begins: Guru Nanak opens the morning raga by saying nothing happens outside the One.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Bhairao, the raga's name as the Granth's heading writes it.

carryVoice: Bhairao: the morning raga that starts by making the room bigger. Nobody is standing outside it. See you tomorrow.
